title: Generalized Ballot Problem: k-Fold Dominance
description: The generalized ballot problem: in an election where candidate A must maintain more than k times the votes of candidate B throughout counting, the probability is (a - kb)/(a + b). Formalized using lattice paths and cyclic rotations.

meta.author: Bertrand (1887), generalized by Dvoretzky-Motzkin (1947)
originalContributions: Generalized ballot sequence definition for arbitrary k-fold dominance
Lattice path model with +1 upsteps and -k downsteps
Prefix sum relation for cyclic rotations (both wrapping and non-wrapping cases)
Connection to classical ballot problem (k=1 reduction)

overview.historicalContext: The classical Ballot Problem was posed by Joseph Bertrand in 1887: if candidate A receives p votes and B receives q votes (p > q), the probability that A leads throughout counting is (p-q)/(p+q). This was first proved by Desire Andre using the reflection principle. In 1947, Dvoretzky and Motzkin proved the Cycle Lemma, which gives a more general and elegant proof applicable to the k-fold generalization.
overview.problemStatement:
**Generalized Ballot Theorem**: In an election where candidate A receives $a$ votes and candidate B receives $b$ votes, with $a > kb$ for a positive integer $k$, the probability that A always has more than $k$ times as many votes as B throughout the counting is:

$$P = \frac{a - kb}{a + b}$$

When $k = 1$, this reduces to the classical formula $P = (p-q)/(p+q)$.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Lattice Path Model + Cycle Lemma**:

1. Model vote counting as a lattice path: each A-vote is a +1 step, each B-vote is a $-k$ step
2. The condition 'A has > k times B's votes' equals the path staying strictly above the x-axis
3. Use the Dvoretzky-Motzkin Cycle Lemma: for a sequence with positive sum $S$ and length $n$, exactly $S$ of the $n$ cyclic rotations have all positive prefix sums
4. Apply to ballot sequences: $S = a - kb$, $n = a + b$, giving the fraction of good orderings
keyInsights: The Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma unifies all ballot-type results: exactly $S$ of $n$ cyclic rotations have all positive prefix sums
Cyclic rotation preserves the multiset of values, so all rotations of a ballot sequence remain in $\text{kCountedSequence}(a, b, k)$
The prefix sum of rotation $i$ at position $j$ satisfies $\sigma_{\text{rot}}(j) = \sigma(i+j) - \sigma(i)$ (non-wrapping) or $\sigma(i+j-n) + S - \sigma(i)$ (wrapping)
The permutation characterization $l \sim \text{replicate}(a, 1) \mathbin{++} \text{replicate}(b, -k)$ enables finiteness via Mathlib's `List.finite_permutations`

sections.title: Generalized Ballot Sequences
sections.summary: Definitions of kCountedSequence (lists with a +1s and b -k values) and kStaysPositive (all prefix sums positive).

sections.title: Core Algebraic Lemmas
sections.summary: Sum and length identities for binary-valued lists: sum = count(1) - k*count(-k), length = count(1) + count(-k).

sections.title: Basic Properties
sections.summary: Sum, length, permutation characterization, finiteness, and nonemptiness of kCountedSequence.

sections.title: Connection to Classical Ballot Problem
sections.summary: When k=1, kCountedSequence equals Mathlib's countedSequence, connecting to the classical result.

sections.title: The Generalized Ballot Theorem
sections.summary: Statement of the counting theorem and probability formula, with verified special cases.
sections.mathContext: $P(\text{A leads throughout}) = \frac{a - kb}{a + b}$ for $a > kb$

sections.title: Cyclic Rotation Infrastructure
sections.summary: Definition and properties of cyclic rotations: sum/length preservation, membership, composition.

sections.title: Prefix Sum Relations
sections.summary: Key structural lemma relating prefix sums of cyclic rotations to prefix sums of the original sequence.

sections.title: The Cycle Lemma
sections.summary: Statement of the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma (1947): for positive-sum sequences, exactly S of n rotations have all positive prefix sums.
sections.mathContext: $|\{i < n \mid \forall j \leq n,\; \sigma_{\text{rot}(i)}(j) > 0\}| = S$ where $S = \sum l > 0$

sections.title: Lattice Path Interpretation
sections.summary: Physical interpretation of ballot sequences as lattice paths with height tracking.
sections.mathContext: Lattice path: A-vote = $(1, 1)$ step, B-vote = $(1, -k)$ step; path stays above $x$-axis iff all prefix sums positive

conclusion.summary: This formalization establishes a comprehensive framework for the generalized ballot problem, building from basic list combinatorics through cyclic rotation theory to the statement of the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma. The key infrastructure - including the prefix sum relation for rotations - is complete, providing the foundation needed to prove the cycle lemma and derive the counting formula.
conclusion.implications:
**Applications:**

1. **Voting theory**: Probability of sustained dominance in elections
2. **Queueing theory**: Probability that a queue never empties (k-server variant)
3. **Random walks**: Paths with asymmetric step sizes staying above a barrier
4. **Lattice path enumeration**: Counting paths with generalized step constraints
openQuestions: Complete proof of the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma in Lean 4
Weighted voting with non-uniform step sizes
